claims.claim: Migration is the permanent or semi-permanent movement of people from one place of residence to another; a person leaving is an emigrant and a person arriving is an immigrant.
Internal migration is movement within a country's borders, while international migration crosses national borders.
Net migration is the difference between the number of immigrants and the number of emigrants for an area in a given period; a positive value means more people arrived than left.
Forced migration involves an element of coercion, such as conflict or disaster, whereas voluntary migration reflects the mover's own choice; the two form a spectrum rather than a strict binary.
Chain migration is movement built on social networks, in which people follow family or community members who have already settled at a destination, often producing clustered ethnic enclaves.
Step migration, a concept from E.G. Ravenstein (1885), describes migration that proceeds in stages, as movers relocate through intermediate-sized places toward larger urban centers.

E.G. Ravenstein set out 'laws of migration' in the 1880s observing that most migration is short-distance and stepwise, that long-distance migrants tend to move to major economic centers, and that each migration flow produces a counterflow; these are best treated as an early empirical framework rather than deterministic laws.
The United Nations estimated about 304 million international migrants worldwide in 2024, roughly 3.7 percent of the global population, up from an estimated 154 million (2.9 percent) in 1990.
The UN defines an international migrant as any person who has changed his or her country of usual residence, regardless of legal status or the reason for the move.
UNHCR reported that about 117.3 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide at the end of 2023, including roughly 43.4 million refugees and 68.3 million internally displaced people.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which figure best represents the scale of international migration.
positions: IOM's World Migration Report 2024 cites about 281 million international migrants in 2020.
UN DESA's more recent estimate is about 304 million in 2024.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Use the most recent UN DESA estimate (304 million, 2024) and attribute it with its year; note the figure grows over time and should never be stated undated.
